Why Sourdough Starters Fail in Winter

By Priya Chandrasekaran — January 14, 2026

Every year, around the first hard frost, my email fills up with the same question: why has a starter that thrived all summer suddenly gone flat and sluggish? The answer almost always comes down to temperature, and the fix is usually simpler than bakers expect.

Wild yeast and the lactic acid bacteria that live alongside it are both temperature-sensitive organisms. Below about eighteen degrees Celsius, their metabolic rate drops sharply, and fermentation that took four hours in July can stretch to ten or twelve hours in January. Bakers who keep feeding on the same schedule they used in summer end up starving a starter that simply has not had time to build up enough gas and acid.

The first thing I ask people to check is where the jar actually lives. A counter near an exterior wall, a drafty windowsill, or a spot directly above a cold tile floor can run five to eight degrees colder than the rest of the kitchen. Moving the jar to the top of the refrigerator, near a running oven light, or into a turned-off microwave with the door closed can make an enormous difference without spending a cent.

If relocating the jar is not enough, the next lever is hydration and feeding ratio. A stiffer starter, fed at something like a 1:1:0.75 flour-to-water ratio, ferments faster in cold rooms than a loose, high-hydration starter does, because there is simply less water to slow down enzymatic activity. I also recommend dropping the feeding ratio itself, from a strict 1:5:5 down to 1:2:2, so the population of yeast and bacteria does not have to grow as far to reach peak activity within the same window of time.

Finally, resist the urge to throw out a winter starter that looks sluggish after only one or two feedings. Given a stable, slightly warmer environment and a week of consistent feeding, nearly every starter I have heard about has recovered fully by the time the next loaf goes into the oven.
